Effectual
ĕf-fĕk´tū-al
adj. (producing the effect intended; in theology, of the call that infallibly brings the sinner to Christ)
Latin efficere, to work out, accomplish. An effectual thing is not merely aimed but lands; the theological term names a call that arrives.

Biblical Definition

The Authorized Version uses the word of prayer — “The effectual fervent prayer of a righteous man availeth much” (Jas 5:16) — of an opened opportunity, “a great door and effectual is opened unto me, and there are many adversaries” (1Co 16:9), and of the gospel's working in the church (Eph 3:7; Eph 4:16; Phm 1:6). In theology effectual calling names the inward call that always arrives: “whom he did predestinate, them he also called: and whom he called, them he also justified” (Rom 8:30), an unbroken chain; and “All that the Father giveth me shall come to me” (John 6:37). The outward call may be refused; this one is the demonstration of “Christ the power of God, and the wisdom of God” (1Co 1:24).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines effectual as producing an effect, or the effect desired or intended; or having adequate power or force to produce the effect.

expand to see more

EFFECTUAL, a. Producing an effect, or the effect desired or intended; or having adequate power or force to produce the effect.

EFFECTUAL CALLING, in theology, that operation of the Holy Spirit by which the sinner is renewed and brought to Christ.

Key Scripture

Jas 5:16 — "Confess your faults one to another, and pray one for another, that ye may be healed. The effectual fervent prayer of a righteous man availeth much."

Rom 8:30 — "Moreover whom he did predestinate, them he also called: and whom he called, them he also justified: and whom he justified, them he also glorified."

John 6:37 — "All that the Father giveth me shall come to me; and him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out."

1Co 1:24 — "But unto them which are called, both Jews and Greeks, Christ the power of God, and the wisdom of God."

1Co 16:9 — "For a great door and effectual is opened unto me, and there are many adversaries."

Modern Corruption

Effectual calling is heard as coercion, and the doctrine is that a man is made willing rather than dragged.

expand to see more

The old name for the doctrine was irresistible grace, and the word has done more harm than the teaching, because it suggests a man hauled to Christ against his will. The Confession is careful in a way the slogan is not: the effectually called are drawn to Jesus Christ, yet so as they come most freely, being made willing by His grace. The change is in the wanting. Nobody is saved reluctantly; the point of the doctrine is that the will itself, which was dead, is made alive, so that the man now desires what he formerly refused and comes without being forced.

Romans 8:30 is a chain with no dropped links, and it is the strongest single argument for the doctrine: whom He predestinated He called, whom He called He justified, whom He justified He glorified — the same company all the way through, and the calling in the middle must therefore be the kind that does not fail, since the number that arrives at glory equals the number that set out. That is not a Calvinist gloss on the verse; it is its grammar.

James 5:16 keeps the word from becoming abstract, and it corrects a common misuse in the other direction. The effectual prayer is not effectual because it is loud or long; the adjective attaches to a prayer that is energised, and the verse's own qualification is the character of the man praying. Effectual, in Scripture, is never about the force applied. It is about who is behind it.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek energeo (G1754), to work, be operative; energeia (G1753), working; kaleo (G2564), to call; kletos (G2822), called.

expand to see more

Greek energeo (G1754) — to be effectual, work; James 5:16, Galatians 2:8, Philippians 2:13.

Greek energeia (G1753) — effectual working; Ephesians 3:7, 4:16, Colossians 1:29.

Greek kaleo (G2564) — to call; Romans 8:30, 1 Corinthians 1:9, 2 Timothy 1:9; kletos (G2822), 1 Corinthians 1:24.

Usage

"“Whom he called, them he also justified” — a chain with no dropped links."

"“They come most freely, being made willing by his grace” — the Confession, against the slogan."

"“A great door and effectual… and there are many adversaries” — both clauses at once."
